P.title: P.blurb
Engineering: Forces, machines and the shapes that keep structures standing.

P.title: me-forces.summary
Engineering: Why a long spanner works, and how machines trade force for distance.

P.title: me-forces.q0.q
Engineering: A 50 kg person stands on a scale. Their weight is about…

P.title: me-forces.q1.q
Engineering: 4 kg sits 1.5 m from the pivot. How far from the pivot must 2 kg sit to balance?

P.title: me-forces.q2.q
Engineering: A 12-tooth gear drives a 36-tooth gear. The output turns…

P.title: me-forces.q2.x
Engineering: The ratio is 36 ÷ 12 = 3: one third of the speed, three times the torque.

P.title: me-forces.q3.q
Engineering: To lift 200 kg by 1 m with a 5 m ramp (no friction) you need about…

P.title: me-forces.q4.q
Engineering: A torque wrench set to 120 N·m with a 0.4 m handle needs a force of…

P.title: me-forces.c0.text
Engineering: A force makes a mass accelerate. Weight is just the force of gravity on a mass: W = m × g, with g ≈ 9.81 m/s² on Earth. Mass is measured in kg; force and weight in newtons (N).

P.title: me-forces.c1.text
Engineering: Turning effect, or torque, is force × distance from the pivot. A small force far from the pivot balances a large force close to it.\n\nThat's why a long spanner loosens a stuck bolt, and why door handles sit far from the hinges.

P.title: me-forces.c2.text
Engineering: The right side holds 6 kg at 1 m from the pivot. Change the mass and distance on the left until the beam levels out.

P.title: me-forces.c3.text
Engineering: With a moving pulley, the load hangs from two strands of rope, so each strand carries half the weight. You pull with half the force, but you have to pull twice as much rope.\n\nThe work you do, force × distance, stays the same. Machines never give energy for free; they let you choose how to spend it.

P.title: me-forces.c4.text
Engineering: When a small gear drives a big one, the big gear turns slower but with more torque. The ratio is the number of teeth: 10 teeth driving 20 gives half the speed and twice the torque.\n\nA bike's low gear, a drill's gearbox and a car's first gear all use this trade.

P.title: me-forces.c5.text
Engineering: When forces on an object balance, it stays still or keeps moving at a steady speed. When they don't, it accelerates in the direction of the net force.

P.title: me-forces.c6.text
Engineering: A ramp lets you raise a load with less force by pushing it over a longer distance. The force needed is roughly the weight times the height divided by the length.

P.title: me-forces.c6.example.0
Engineering: Lift 100 kg 1 m using a 4 m ramp

P.title: me-forces.c7.text
Engineering: A screw is a ramp wrapped around a cylinder: each turn moves it forward a little with great force. A wedge (an axe, a chisel) turns a push into a sideways splitting force.

P.title: me-forces.c8.text
Engineering: Mechanical advantage is output force divided by input force. A lever with MA = 5 lets you lift 5 times what you push, but you move 5 times farther.

P.title: me-forces.c9.text
Engineering: Bolts are tightened to a specified torque in newton-metres. A wheel nut on a car is often around 100–140 N·m: 400 N on a 30 cm wrench gives 120 N·m.

P.title: me-structures.summary
Engineering: Tension, compression and the shapes engineers use to manage them.

P.title: me-structures.q0.q
Engineering: A simply supported beam carries a load in the middle. Where is it in tension?

P.title: me-structures.q0.x
Engineering: It sags, so the bottom stretches (tension) and the top squeezes (compression).

P.title: me-structures.q1.q
Engineering: Why are trusses made of triangles?

P.title: me-structures.q1.o0
Engineering: They use less steel than squares

P.title: me-structures.q1.o1
Engineering: A triangle can't deform without a side changing length

P.title: me-structures.q1.x
Engineering: Fixed side lengths lock a triangle's angles, so pinned joints alone keep it rigid.

P.title: me-structures.q2.q
Engineering: Rope with a breaking load of 600 kg, used with a factor of safety of 5. Max working load?

P.title: me-structures.q2.x
Engineering: Working load = failure load ÷ FoS = 600 ÷ 5 = 120 kg.

P.title: me-structures.q3.q
Engineering: A balcony fixed only at the wall is a…

P.title: me-structures.q4.q
Engineering: What usually makes a tall slender column fail?

P.title: me-structures.c0.text
Engineering: Load a beam in the middle and it bends. The top gets squeezed (compression) and the bottom gets stretched (tension). Somewhere in between is a neutral line that feels neither.\n\nConcrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, which is why beams have steel bars near the bottom.

P.title: me-structures.c1.text
Engineering: Push the corner of a square frame and it folds into a parallelogram; the joints just rotate. A triangle can't change shape without changing the length of a side.\n\nThat's why cranes, roof trusses, pylons and bike frames are made of triangles.

P.title: me-structures.c2.text
Engineering: An arch turns a downward load into compression that runs around its curve to the ground. Stone, which is strong in compression, is perfect for it.\n\nThe catch is that the feet push outward. Without solid abutments or a tie between the feet, the arch spreads and collapses.

P.title: me-structures.c3.text
Engineering: When a beam bends, the most stress is at the top and bottom faces and very little in the middle. An I-beam puts most of its steel in the top and bottom flanges and joins them with a thin web.\n\nYou get almost the stiffness of a solid block with a fraction of the weight.

P.title: me-structures.c4.text
Engineering: Engineers never design right up to the breaking point. Materials vary, loads get underestimated and things wear out. The factor of safety is how much stronger something is than it needs to be.\n\nLifting gear often uses 4 or 5; aircraft structures use about 1.5, because extra weight costs fuel and every part is tested closely.

P.title: me-structures.c4.example.0
Engineering: Hook rated for 1 t, breaks at 4 t

P.title: me-structures.c5.text
Engineering: A cantilever is supported at one end only: balconies, diving boards, shelf brackets. The top is in tension and the bottom in compression, the opposite of a simply supported beam.

P.title: me-structures.c6.text
Engineering: A tall slender column doesn't crush; it buckles sideways first. Doubling its length can cut its buckling load to a quarter, which is why columns are braced.

P.title: me-structures.c7.text
Engineering: Curved shells spread loads through their surface, like an eggshell. Domes from the Pantheon in Rome to modern stadiums cover huge spaces with little material.

P.title: me-structures.c8.text
Engineering: Every load must travel down through the structure to the ground: floor to beams, beams to columns, columns to foundations. If any link is missing, something fails.

P.title: me-structures.c9.text
Engineering: Engineers design for dead load (the structure's own weight), live load (people, furniture, snow), and environmental loads like wind and earthquakes, then add safety factors.

P.title: me-materials.summary
Engineering: Steel, concrete, wood, aluminium and plastics.

P.title: me-materials.q0.q
Engineering: Why does reinforced concrete contain steel bars?

P.title: me-materials.q0.o1
Engineering: Concrete is weak in tension, so steel carries the tensile forces

P.title: me-materials.q2.q
Engineering: Which is the lightest per volume?

P.title: me-materials.q2.x
Engineering: Aluminium is about a third of steel's density.

P.title: me-materials.c0.text
Engineering: Strength is how much stress a material takes before it breaks or yields. Stiffness is how much it resists bending or stretching. Rubber is weak and flexible; glass is stiff but brittle.

P.title: me-materials.c0.viz.r.items.1
Engineering: steel stiff, aluminium a third as stiff

P.title: me-materials.c1.text
Engineering: Steel is iron with a little carbon. It's strong in both tension and compression, ductile (bends before breaking) and recyclable, but heavy and rusts without protection.

P.title: me-materials.c2.text
Engineering: Concrete is cement, water, sand and gravel. It's cheap and very strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel bars (rebar) are added where tension occurs.

P.title: me-materials.c3.text
Engineering: Wood is strong along the grain and weak across it. For its weight it's remarkably strong, it stores carbon and is easy to work, but moisture, fire and insects must be managed.

P.title: me-materials.c4.text
Engineering: Aluminium is about a third the weight of steel and doesn't rust (a thin oxide layer protects it). It's less stiff, so parts are made thicker or shaped cleverly. Used in aircraft, window frames, cars.

P.title: me-materials.c5.text
Engineering: Plastics are light, cheap and mouldable. Composites like carbon fibre embed strong fibres in resin, giving very high strength and stiffness for their weight: bikes, aircraft, racing cars.

P.title: me-materials.c6.text
Engineering: Engineers weigh strength, stiffness, weight, cost, durability, ease of manufacture and environmental impact. There's never a perfect material, only the best compromise.

P.title: me-materials.c7.text
Engineering: Making cement releases a lot of CO₂, about 8% of global emissions according to many estimates. Steel production is also carbon-heavy. That's driving interest in timber buildings and low-carbon cements.

P.title: me-materials.c8.text
Engineering: Steel rusts when exposed to oxygen and water, especially with salt. Protection includes paint, galvanising (zinc coating), stainless alloys and keeping concrete cover over rebar.

P.title: me-materials.c9.text
Engineering: Glass is very strong in compression but brittle: a tiny scratch can start a crack. Tempered glass is heat-treated to be much stronger and shatters into small blunt pieces; laminated glass holds together.

P.title: me-stress.summary
Engineering: How materials stretch, bend and break.

P.title: me-stress.q0.q
Engineering: 20 kN on a 400 mm² bar gives a stress of…

P.title: me-stress.q1.q
Engineering: Turning a plank on edge makes it much stiffer because…

P.title: me-stress.q1.o1
Engineering: Bending stiffness grows with depth cubed

P.title: me-stress.q2.q
Engineering: Which material gives warning before breaking?

P.title: me-stress.c0.text
Engineering: Stress is force divided by the area carrying it. The same force on a thinner bar creates more stress. Units: pascals (N/m²), usually megapascals (MPa).

P.title: me-stress.c0.example.0
Engineering: 10 kN on a 100 mm² steel bar

P.title: me-stress.c1.text
Engineering: Strain is how much a material stretches compared with its original length. It has no units and is usually tiny.

P.title: me-stress.c2.text
Engineering: Stiffness is measured by Young's modulus: stress divided by strain. Steel is about 200 GPa, aluminium about 70, wood about 10 along the grain.

P.title: me-stress.c3.text
Engineering: In the elastic range, a material springs back when unloaded. Past the yield point it deforms permanently (plastic). Engineers design structures to stay elastic in normal use.

P.title: me-stress.c4.text
Engineering: Testing a steel bar in a machine draws a curve: a straight elastic line, a yield point, then plastic stretching up to the ultimate strength, and finally fracture.

P.title: me-stress.c5.text
Engineering: Ductile materials (steel, copper) stretch a lot before breaking, giving warning. Brittle ones (glass, cast iron, concrete) snap suddenly. Ductility makes structures safer.

P.title: me-stress.c6.text
Engineering: When a beam bends, stress is zero at the middle (neutral axis) and greatest at the top and bottom surfaces. That's why I-beams put material far from the middle.

P.title: me-stress.c7.text
Engineering: A beam's resistance to bending depends hugely on its depth. For a rectangle, doubling the depth makes it eight times stiffer. That's why joists are placed on edge.

P.title: me-stress.c8.text
Engineering: Materials grow when heated. A 100 m steel bridge can lengthen about 4 cm between winter and summer, so it has expansion joints. Rails, pipes and concrete slabs need room to move too.

P.title: me-stress.c9.text
Engineering: Sharp corners, holes and notches concentrate stress, sometimes to three times the average. Rounded corners (fillets) spread it out. Aircraft windows are rounded for this reason.

P.title: me-stress.c9.viz.items.1.w
Engineering: square window in a pressurised cabin

P.title: me-friction.summary
Engineering: The force that grips, slows and wears things down.

P.title: me-friction.q0.q
Engineering: A 50 kg box (≈490 N) on a floor with μ = 0.4 needs about how much force to slide?

P.title: me-friction.q1.q
Engineering: Why is it harder to start pushing a box than to keep it moving?

P.title: me-friction.q1.o1
Engineering: Static friction is higher than kinetic friction

P.title: me-friction.q1.x
Engineering: Starting needs to overcome static friction.

P.title: me-friction.q2.x
Engineering: Rolling resists far less than sliding.

P.title: me-friction.c0.text
Engineering: Friction resists sliding between surfaces. At a microscopic level, even smooth surfaces are rough, and bumps catch and briefly bond.

P.title: me-friction.c1.text
Engineering: Friction force is roughly the normal force (how hard surfaces press together) times a coefficient μ that depends on the materials.

P.title: me-friction.c2.text
Engineering: It takes more force to start something sliding than to keep it going. Static friction is higher than kinetic (sliding) friction. That's why ABS keeps wheels from locking.

P.title: me-friction.c3.text
Engineering: Brakes turn motion into heat through friction between pads and discs. On a long descent, brakes can overheat and fade; using engine braking or EV regeneration helps.

P.title: me-friction.c4.text
Engineering: Tyres grip through friction and slight deformation of the rubber. On wet roads, tread grooves channel water away; without them, the tyre can aquaplane on a water film.

P.title: me-friction.c5.text
Engineering: Oil and grease separate surfaces with a thin film, cutting friction and wear dramatically. Engines, bearings and gearboxes depend on it.

P.title: me-friction.c6.text
Engineering: Ball and roller bearings replace sliding with rolling, which has far lower friction. They're in wheels, motors, fans and hard drives.

P.title: me-friction.c7.text
Engineering: Without friction you couldn't walk, drive, hold a pen or keep a nut on a bolt. Engineers often add friction on purpose: clutch plates, belt drives, non-slip floors.

P.title: me-friction.c8.text
Engineering: Even rolling tyres lose energy as the rubber flexes. Low-rolling-resistance tyres and correct pressure save fuel or EV range.

P.title: me-friction.c9.text
Engineering: Friction and wear are estimated to consume around a fifth of the world's energy and cause large losses through worn parts, according to tribology studies. Better lubricants and materials save a lot.

P.title: me-friction.c9.viz.items.0.l
Engineering: of world energy used to overcome friction (estimate)

P.title: me-energy.summary
Engineering: Lifting, moving and how fast it happens.

P.title: me-energy.q0.q
Engineering: Kinetic energy at 100 km/h compared with 50 km/h is…

P.title: me-energy.q1.q
Engineering: Lifting 20 kg by 2 m does about how much work?

P.title: me-energy.c0.text
Engineering: Work is done when a force moves something: force times distance. Lift a 10 kg bag 1 m and you do about 98 J of work.

P.title: me-energy.c1.text
Engineering: Raising something stores energy that can be released when it falls. Hydroelectric dams use this with millions of tonnes of water.

P.title: me-energy.c2.text
Engineering: Moving objects carry energy that grows with the square of speed. Double the speed and the energy quadruples, which is why speed matters so much in crashes.

P.title: me-energy.c2.example.0
Engineering: 1,500 kg car at 50 km/h vs 100 km/h

P.title: me-energy.c3.text
Engineering: Power is how fast work is done: joules per second, or watts. A strong cyclist sustains about 200–300 W; a car engine delivers tens to hundreds of kW.

P.title: me-energy.c4.text
Engineering: James Watt defined horsepower to sell steam engines: about 746 W in the imperial version. The metric horsepower (cv in Portugal) is about 735 W.

P.title: me-energy.c5.text
Engineering: No machine converts all input energy into useful output; some becomes heat or noise. Efficiency is useful output divided by input.

P.title: me-energy.c6.text
Engineering: Energy changes form but the total stays the same. A falling roller coaster turns potential energy into kinetic energy, then back again, minus friction losses.

P.title: me-energy.c6.viz.steps.0
Engineering: Top of the hill: potential energy

P.title: me-energy.c7.text
Engineering: Engineers use joules; electricity bills use kWh. One kWh is 3.6 million joules, the energy of a 1 kW heater running for an hour.

P.title: me-energy.c8.text
Engineering: A litre of petrol holds about 9 kWh of chemical energy, which is why liquid fuels were so hard to beat. Lithium batteries hold far less per kilo, but electric drivetrains use energy much more efficiently.

P.title: me-energy.c9.text
Engineering: A spring stores energy when stretched or compressed. Its force is proportional to how far it moves (Hooke's law), used in suspensions, scales and clocks.

P.title: me-fluids.summary
Engineering: Pressure, buoyancy and the power of liquids.

P.title: me-fluids.q0.q
Engineering: Roughly how much does pressure increase per 10 m of water depth?

P.title: me-fluids.q1.q
Engineering: A hydraulic jack with an area ratio of 20 turns 50 N into…

P.title: me-fluids.q2.q
Engineering: Why does a steel ship float?

P.title: me-fluids.q2.o1
Engineering: Its shape displaces a weight of water greater than its own

P.title: me-fluids.c0.text
Engineering: Pressure is force spread over an area. A stiletto heel presses far harder on the floor than an elephant's foot, because the area is tiny.

P.title: me-fluids.c1.text
Engineering: Water pressure increases with depth, about 1 bar every 10 metres. Divers feel it in their ears; dams are thicker at the bottom for the same reason.

P.title: me-fluids.c2.text
Engineering: Air above us presses down with about 1 bar (101 kPa) at sea level, roughly 10 tonnes on every square metre. We don't notice because it pushes equally from all sides.

P.title: me-fluids.c3.text
Engineering: Pressure in a closed liquid spreads equally in all directions. Push a small piston and a big piston feels the same pressure over a larger area, giving a bigger force.

P.title: me-fluids.c4.text
Engineering: Car brakes, excavators, lifts and presses use hydraulic fluid to multiply force and transmit it through flexible hoses.

P.title: me-fluids.c5.text
Engineering: An object in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces (Archimedes). If that's more than its own weight, it floats. Steel ships float because their shape displaces a lot of water.

P.title: me-fluids.c6.text
Engineering: Flow rate equals speed times pipe area. Squeeze a hose and the water speeds up. Narrow pipes need more pressure to push the same flow because of friction.

P.title: me-fluids.c7.text
Engineering: Where a fluid moves faster, its pressure drops. This helps explain carburettors, atomisers and part of how wings and sails create lift.

P.title: me-fluids.c8.text
Engineering: A siphon moves liquid up over a barrier and down to a lower point without a pump, as long as the outlet is below the source and the tube starts full.

P.title: me-fluids.c9.text
Engineering: Viscosity is a fluid's thickness: honey is viscous, water isn't. Oil grades like 5W-30 describe how viscosity behaves when cold (5W) and hot (30).

P.title: me-flight.q0.o1
Engineering: The wing's airflow separates and lift drops sharply

P.title: me-flight.q0.x
Engineering: Too high an angle of attack.

P.title: me-flight.q1.q
Engineering: Doubling speed changes drag by a factor of about…

P.title: me-flight.q2.q
Engineering: Which control surface rolls the plane?

P.title: me-flight.q2.x
Engineering: Ailerons move in opposite directions on each wing.

P.title: me-flight.c0.text
Engineering: In steady flight, lift balances weight and thrust balances drag. To climb, lift exceeds weight; to speed up, thrust exceeds drag.

P.title: me-flight.c1.text
Engineering: A wing is shaped and tilted (angle of attack) to deflect air downwards. Pushing air down pushes the wing up (Newton's third law), with lower pressure above the wing and higher below.

P.title: me-flight.c2.text
Engineering: Lift grows with air density, wing area and the square of speed. That's why planes need long runways at hot, high airports where air is thin.

P.title: me-flight.c2.viz.f
Engineering: L = ½ × ρ × v² × S × CL

P.title: me-flight.c3.text
Engineering: Increase the angle of attack too much and the airflow separates from the upper surface. Lift collapses suddenly: a stall. Pilots train to recognise and recover from it.

P.title: me-flight.c4.text
Engineering: For take-off and landing, flaps and slats extend from the wing to increase its area and curvature, giving more lift at low speed.

P.title: me-flight.c5.text
Engineering: Drag comes from friction with the air and from the pressure difference behind the object. It grows with the square of speed, so going faster costs a lot more fuel.

P.title: me-flight.c6.text
Engineering: A turbofan sucks in air, compresses it, burns fuel in it and blasts the hot gas out the back. Most thrust in airliners comes from the big fan pushing air around the core.

P.title: me-flight.c6.viz.steps.3
Engineering: Turbine and exhaust push the plane

P.title: me-flight.c7.text
Engineering: At about 10–12 km altitude, the air is thin, so drag is much lower and jet engines are more efficient. Cabins are pressurised to the equivalent of about 2,000 m.

P.title: me-flight.c8.text
Engineering: Ailerons on the wings roll the plane, the elevator on the tail pitches it up and down, and the rudder yaws it left and right.

P.title: me-flight.c9.text
Engineering: Multirotor drones have no wings; they create lift by spinning propellers. They steer by speeding up some motors and slowing others, with a flight controller adjusting hundreds of times a second.

P.title: me-bridges.q0.q
Engineering: Which bridge type carries loads mainly in compression?

P.title: me-bridges.q1.q
Engineering: Lisbon's 25 de Abril bridge is a…

P.title: me-bridges.q2.q
Engineering: What destroyed the Tacoma Narrows bridge in 1940?

P.title: me-bridges.c0.text
Engineering: Bridges handle loads differently: beams bend, arches compress, suspension cables pull, and cable-stayed towers hold the deck with straight cables.

P.title: me-bridges.c1.text
Engineering: The simplest bridge: a beam on supports. Cheap and quick for short spans, but deep beams are needed as the span grows, so they're often continuous over many piers.

P.title: me-bridges.c2.text
Engineering: Arches carry loads in compression to strong abutments. Stone arches have lasted for 2,000 years. Porto's Dom Luís I bridge (1886) is a double-deck iron arch over the Douro.

P.title: me-bridges.c3.text
Engineering: Main cables hang from tall towers and are anchored at each end; vertical hangers hold the deck. They achieve the longest spans. Lisbon's 25 de Abril bridge (1966) is one.

P.title: me-bridges.c4.text
Engineering: Straight cables run directly from towers to the deck in a fan or harp pattern. Efficient for medium-long spans and quick to build. Lisbon's Vasco da Gama bridge has a cable-stayed main span.

P.title: me-bridges.c5.text
Engineering: Portugal has some remarkable bridges, including several by Gustave Eiffel's company and Edgar Cardoso.

P.title: me-bridges.c6.text
Engineering: In 1940 the Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge in the US twisted itself apart in a moderate wind, due to aerodynamic instability. Since then, decks are wind-tunnel tested and shaped to avoid it.

P.title: me-bridges.c7.text
Engineering: Bridges grow and shrink with temperature. Expansion joints (the metal teeth you drive over) and sliding bearings let them move without cracking.

P.title: me-bridges.c8.text
Engineering: Piers in rivers must resist scour: fast water digging away the riverbed around them. Many bridge failures come from scour during floods, not from the structure itself.

P.title: me-bridges.c8.viz.steps.0
Engineering: Flood water speeds up around pier

P.title: me-bridges.c9.text
Engineering: Bridges are inspected regularly for cracks, corrosion, bearing wear and scour. Sensors increasingly monitor strain, vibration and movement in real time.

P.title: me-buildings.q0.o1
Engineering: One part of a building sinking more than another

P.title: me-buildings.q1.o1
Engineering: A timber lattice inside walls for earthquake resistance

P.title: me-buildings.q2.o0
Engineering: On solid rock near the surface

P.title: me-buildings.q2.o1
Engineering: On soft ground, to reach firmer layers

P.title: me-buildings.q2.x
Engineering: They transfer loads to deeper strata.

P.title: me-buildings.c0.text
Engineering: Foundations spread a building's weight onto soil that can carry it without sinking unevenly. The weaker the soil, the bigger or deeper the foundations.

P.title: me-buildings.c1.text
Engineering: Strip and pad footings, or a raft slab, work where firm soil or rock is near the surface. They're common for houses.

P.title: me-buildings.c2.text
Engineering: On soft ground, piles are driven or drilled down to firmer layers, carrying loads by end bearing and friction along their sides. Lisbon's Baixa was rebuilt after 1755 on wooden piles.

P.title: me-buildings.c3.text
Engineering: All buildings settle a little. Problems come from differential settlement, when one part sinks more than another, cracking walls and jamming doors.

P.title: me-buildings.c4.text
Engineering: Traditional buildings have load-bearing walls of stone or brick. Modern ones use frames of concrete or steel columns and beams, with walls just filling the gaps.

P.title: me-buildings.c5.text
Engineering: After the 1755 earthquake, Lisbon was rebuilt with the "gaiola pombalina": a timber lattice of diagonal braces inside masonry walls, one of the first earthquake-resistant building systems in Europe.

P.title: me-buildings.c6.text
Engineering: Seismic codes require buildings to sway without collapsing: ductile connections, bracing, shear walls, regular shapes. Some use base isolators that let the ground move beneath them.

P.title: me-buildings.c7.text
Engineering: Wind pushes on tall buildings and makes them sway. Engineers stiffen them with cores and outriggers, and some skyscrapers use giant tuned mass dampers to cancel motion.

P.title: me-buildings.c8.text
Engineering: Water is the enemy of buildings: rising damp, leaks and condensation cause rot, mould and corrosion. Damp-proof courses, good roofs, gutters and ventilation keep it out.

P.title: me-buildings.c9.text
Engineering: The world's tallest building, in Dubai, is 828 m high. Its Y-shaped plan and setbacks confuse the wind, and its foundations include 192 piles about 50 m long.

P.title: me-engines.summary
Engineering: How petrol and diesel engines turn fuel into motion.

P.title: me-engines.q0.q
Engineering: What ignites the fuel in a diesel engine?

P.title: me-engines.q1.q
Engineering: What does a turbocharger use to compress intake air?

P.title: me-engines.q2.q
Engineering: Roughly what share of fuel energy becomes useful work in a petrol car engine?

P.title: me-engines.q2.x
Engineering: The rest is lost as heat.

P.title: me-engines.c0.text
Engineering: Most car engines repeat four strokes: suck in air and fuel, squeeze it, ignite it so it pushes the piston, and push out the exhaust. "Suck, squeeze, bang, blow."

P.title: me-engines.c1.text
Engineering: Pistons move up and down; the crankshaft turns that into rotation, like legs pushing bicycle pedals. A flywheel smooths out the pulses.

P.title: me-engines.c2.text
Engineering: Petrol engines use a spark to ignite the mixture. Diesels compress air so much that it gets hot enough to ignite fuel injected into it. Diesels are more efficient but heavier and produce more NOx and particles.

P.title: me-engines.c3.text
Engineering: Higher compression extracts more energy from the fuel. Petrol engines run about 10:1, diesels about 15–20:1. Too high in a petrol engine causes knocking.

P.title: me-engines.c4.text
Engineering: A turbo uses exhaust gas to spin a turbine that compresses intake air, forcing more air and fuel into the cylinders. Small engines can produce big power.

P.title: me-engines.c5.text
Engineering: Torque is the twisting force; power is torque times rotational speed. Diesels deliver strong torque at low rpm; petrol engines often make peak power at high rpm.

P.title: me-engines.c6.text
Engineering: Engines work best in a narrow speed range. Gears let the engine stay in that range whether the car is crawling or cruising. EV motors spin so widely they usually need just one gear.

P.title: me-engines.c6.viz.l.items.1
Engineering: keeps engine in its sweet spot

P.title: me-engines.c7.text
Engineering: About a third of a fuel's energy leaves as heat through the cooling system, and another third through the exhaust. The radiator, coolant and thermostat keep the engine at its ideal temperature.

P.title: me-engines.c8.text
Engineering: Catalytic converters turn carbon monoxide, unburnt fuel and NOx into less harmful gases. Diesel particulate filters trap soot; AdBlue reduces NOx in diesels.

P.title: me-engines.c9.text
Engineering: Hybrids pair a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery, recovering braking energy and helping the engine work efficiently. Plug-in hybrids can drive tens of kilometres on electricity alone.

P.title: me-ev.summary
Engineering: Battery, motor, inverter and thermal management.

P.title: me-ev.q0.q
Engineering: Which part converts the battery's DC into AC for the motor?

P.title: me-ev.q1.q
Engineering: Why do EVs lose range in winter?

P.title: me-ev.q1.o1
Engineering: Cold batteries are less efficient and heating uses energy

P.title: me-ev.q1.x
Engineering: Both chemistry and cabin heating matter.

P.title: me-ev.q2.q
Engineering: What's a typical drag coefficient for an efficient EV?

P.title: me-ev.c0.text
Engineering: An EV has far fewer moving parts than a combustion car: a battery pack, an inverter that turns DC into three-phase AC, an electric motor and a single-speed reduction gear.

P.title: me-ev.c1.text
Engineering: Most EVs mount the battery flat under the floor between the axles. That lowers the centre of gravity, frees cabin space and stiffens the body.

P.title: me-ev.c2.text
Engineering: The inverter switches the battery's DC on and off thousands of times a second with silicon or silicon-carbide transistors to create AC at whatever frequency the motor needs. Silicon carbide cuts losses, especially in 800 V cars.

P.title: me-ev.c3.text
Engineering: Batteries like about 20–40 °C. Liquid cooling plates, heat pumps and pre-conditioning keep them there for fast charging and long life, and reuse waste heat to warm the cabin.

P.title: me-ev.c4.text
Engineering: EV consumption is measured in kWh per 100 km. A compact car may use 14–16; a large SUV 20–24. Speed, cold and wind raise it a lot.

P.title: me-ev.c5.text
Engineering: Cold batteries have higher internal resistance, and heating the cabin takes energy. Range can fall by 20–30% in freezing weather; heat pumps reduce the loss.

P.title: me-ev.c5.viz.items.0
Engineering: Battery chemistry slows in the cold

P.title: me-ev.c6.text
Engineering: At motorway speeds, most energy goes into pushing air. EVs have smooth underbodies, flush handles and low drag coefficients (Cd around 0.2–0.3).

P.title: me-ev.c7.text
Engineering: The motor acts as a generator when slowing down, recovering part of the energy. Friction brakes are still there for hard stops and are used less, so they last much longer.

P.title: me-ev.c8.text
Engineering: No oil changes, spark plugs, clutch, exhaust or timing belt. Maintenance mostly involves tyres, brakes fluid, cabin filters and coolant.

P.title: me-ev.c8.viz.r.items.0
Engineering: tyres, brake fluid, cabin filter, coolant

P.title: me-ev.c9.text
Engineering: Most manufacturers guarantee batteries for about 8 years or 160,000 km, typically to at least 70% capacity. Real-world data shows most packs degrade slowly.

P.title: me-thermo.summary
Engineering: Heat, engines and why nothing is 100% efficient.

P.title: me-thermo.q1.q
Engineering: A heat pump uses work to…

P.title: me-thermo.q1.o1
Engineering: Move heat from a colder place to a warmer one

P.title: me-thermo.q2.q
Engineering: A wall with a lower U-value…

P.title: me-thermo.c0.text
Engineering: Temperature measures how fast molecules jiggle. Heat is energy flowing from hotter to colder because of a temperature difference.

P.title: me-thermo.c1.text
Engineering: Nothing can be colder than −273.15 °C, absolute zero, where molecular motion is at a minimum. The kelvin scale starts there: 0 K.

P.title: me-thermo.c2.text
Engineering: Energy can't be created or destroyed. Heat added to a system goes into raising its internal energy or doing work.

P.title: me-thermo.c3.text
Engineering: Heat flows naturally from hot to cold, never the reverse on its own. Every real process creates some disorder (entropy), which is why no engine can turn all heat into work.

P.title: me-thermo.c4.text
Engineering: The maximum possible efficiency of a heat engine depends only on its hot and cold temperatures, in kelvin.

P.title: me-thermo.c4.example.0
Engineering: Steam at 550 °C (823 K), river at 20 °C (293 K)

P.title: me-thermo.c4.viz.f
Engineering: η max = 1 − T cold ÷ T hot

P.title: me-thermo.c5.text
Engineering: A heat engine uses heat flow to make work. A heat pump does the reverse: uses work to move heat from cold to hot. Same physics, opposite direction.

P.title: me-thermo.c6.text
Engineering: A refrigerant evaporates in the cold side (absorbing heat), is compressed (getting hot), condenses in the hot side (releasing heat) and expands back. Fridges and heat pumps use this loop.

P.title: me-thermo.c7.text
Engineering: Water stores a lot of heat per kilo, which makes it ideal for heating systems and thermal storage tanks. Stone and concrete store heat too: thermal mass keeps old houses cool in summer.

P.title: me-thermo.c8.text
Engineering: Heat loss through walls is measured with U-values: watts lost per m² per degree of difference. Lower is better. A well-insulated modern wall may be below 0.3; an old solid wall can exceed 1.5.

P.title: me-thermo.c9.text
Engineering: Melting ice and boiling water absorb large amounts of energy without changing temperature. Turning 1 kg of water at 100 °C into steam takes about 2.26 MJ, over five times the energy to heat it from 0 to 100 °C.

P.title: me-wood.summary
Engineering: Grain, moisture, joints and timber in construction.

P.title: me-wood.q0.q
Engineering: Why leave room for wood to move in a floor?

P.title: me-wood.q0.o1
Engineering: Wood shrinks and swells with humidity

P.title: me-wood.q1.q
Engineering: Indoor timber should be dried to about…

P.title: me-wood.q2.q
Engineering: Which country is the world's largest cork producer?

P.title: me-wood.q2.x
Engineering: Portugal supplies about half the world's cork.

P.title: me-wood.c0.text
Engineering: Softwoods come from conifers (pine, spruce): fast-growing, light, used for structure. Hardwoods come from broadleaf trees (oak, chestnut, eucalyptus): usually denser and more durable.

P.title: me-wood.c1.text
Engineering: Fresh-cut wood can be over 50% water by weight. It shrinks as it dries until it matches the air's humidity. Indoor timber should be dried to about 8–12% before use.

P.title: me-wood.c2.text
Engineering: Wood shrinks and swells far more across the grain than along it. Doors stick in winter damp, floors gap in dry summers. Good carpentry leaves room for movement.

P.title: me-wood.c3.text
Engineering: Traditional joints interlock pieces so the wood carries the load: mortise and tenon, dovetail, half-lap. Modern work also uses screws, dowels, biscuits and metal connectors.

P.title: me-wood.c4.text
Engineering: Plane and chisel with the grain, like stroking a cat, to avoid tear-out. Knots are weak points and can fall out of thin boards.

P.title: me-wood.c5.text
Engineering: Engineered timber glues layers together. Glulam makes long, strong beams; cross-laminated timber (CLT) panels have layers at right angles and can form walls and floors of multi-storey buildings.

P.title: me-wood.c6.text
Engineering: Rot needs moisture. Keep timber dry, ventilated and off the ground; use naturally durable species or treated wood outdoors. Woodworm and termites are managed with treatment and inspection.

P.title: me-wood.c7.text
Engineering: Thick timber chars on the outside, and the char layer insulates the core, so big beams keep their strength surprisingly long in a fire. Engineers design a char allowance into the sections.

P.title: me-wood.c8.text
Engineering: Traditional Portuguese roofs use timber rafters and battens under ceramic tiles. Trusses spread the roof load to the walls; good ventilation stops condensation rot.

P.title: me-wood.c9.text
Engineering: Eucalyptus, maritime pine and cork oak are Portugal's most common forest trees. Portugal is the world's largest cork producer, supplying roughly half the world's cork.

P.title: me-construction.summary
Engineering: Insulation, windows, thermal bridges and ventilation.

P.title: me-construction.q0.q
Engineering: Where does an uninsulated house often lose a large share of its heat, and is cheap to fix first?

P.title: me-construction.q0.x
Engineering: Roof insulation is usually the best first step.

P.title: me-construction.q1.o1
Engineering: A weak spot where heat bypasses the insulation

P.title: me-construction.q1.x
Engineering: They cause cold spots and mould.

P.title: me-construction.q2.o1
Engineering: Ventilates while recovering heat from outgoing air

P.title: me-construction.c0.text
Engineering: Walls, roof, floor and windows form the envelope that separates inside from outside. Its insulation, airtightness and shading decide how much energy the home needs.

P.title: me-construction.c1.text
Engineering: In an uninsulated house, the roof often loses the most heat, followed by walls, windows and draughts. Insulating the roof first is usually the best value.

P.title: me-construction.c2.text
Engineering: Insulation boards fixed outside the walls and rendered over (the "capoto" system in Portugal) wrap the house in a continuous layer and keep the masonry warm, reducing thermal bridges.

P.title: me-construction.c3.text
Engineering: A thermal bridge is a weak spot where heat bypasses the insulation: concrete beams, balcony slabs, window reveals. They cause cold spots, condensation and mould.

P.title: me-construction.c4.text
Engineering: Double glazing with low-emissivity coating and a thermally broken frame loses far less heat than single glazing. External shading keeps summer sun out before it heats the room.

P.title: me-construction.c5.text
Engineering: Uncontrolled draughts waste heat and carry moisture into walls. Sealing gaps around windows, pipes and roof junctions is cheap and effective.

P.title: me-construction.c6.text
Engineering: A tight house needs controlled ventilation to remove moisture and stale air. Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) recovers most of the heat from the outgoing air.

P.title: me-construction.c7.text
Engineering: Warm indoor air carries moisture; when it meets a cold surface, it condenses. Ventilation, insulation and avoiding cold spots prevent mould.

P.title: me-construction.c8.text
Engineering: In Portugal, keeping cool matters too: external blinds, shading, thermal mass, light colours and night ventilation often beat air conditioning.

P.title: me-construction.c9.text
Engineering: In Portugal, homes for sale or rent need an energy certificate (from A+ to F), issued through ADENE. It also recommends improvements.

P.title: me-water.q0.q
Engineering: About how much pressure is 10 m of water head?

P.title: me-water.q1.o1
Engineering: Sudden valve closure stopping moving water

P.title: me-water.q2.q
Engineering: Why should hot water tanks reach about 60 °C periodically?

P.title: me-water.c0.text
Engineering: Mains water usually arrives at about 2–5 bar. Too low and showers trickle; too high and taps hammer and appliances wear. A pressure-reducing valve fixes high pressure.

P.title: me-water.c1.text
Engineering: Larger pipes carry more flow with less pressure loss. Long runs to an upstairs shower need bigger diameters than a short run to a basin.

P.title: me-water.c1.viz.unit
Engineering: flow at the same pressure loss (relative)

P.title: me-water.c2.text
Engineering: Centrifugal pumps spin an impeller to push water. Each has a curve: more flow means less pressure (head). Choose the pump where its curve meets your system's needs.

P.title: me-water.c3.text
Engineering: Pump "head" is the height it can lift water. 10 m of head equals about 1 bar.

P.title: me-water.c3.viz.items.0.s
Engineering: lift to a tank 20 m up

P.title: me-water.c4.text
Engineering: Closing a valve suddenly stops the flow, and the moving water's momentum creates a pressure spike that bangs pipes. Arrestors and slower-closing valves cure it.

P.title: me-water.c5.text
Engineering: Water heaters store hot water in a tank (termoacumulador), or heat it instantly (gas or electric instantaneous). Solar thermal panels and heat pumps can supply most hot water in Portugal.

P.title: me-water.c6.text
Engineering: Bacteria can grow in stored water between 25 and 45 °C. Storage tanks should reach about 60 °C periodically, and taps should deliver below scalding temperature with mixing valves.

P.title: me-water.c7.text
Engineering: Drains work by gravity, so pipes need a fall (slope) of about 1–2%. Traps (U-bends) hold water to block sewer smells, and vents stop them from being sucked dry.

P.title: me-water.c8.text
Engineering: Collecting roof rainwater for toilets, gardens and washing machines saves mains water. A filter, a tank and a small pump are the main parts.

P.title: me-water.c9.text
Engineering: Tanks and wells are monitored with float switches, pressure sensors or ultrasonic sensors such as the JSN-SR04T, which send levels to a dashboard, even over LoRa from remote sites.

P.title: me-water.c9.viz.steps.0
Engineering: Ultrasonic sensor on the tank lid

P.title: me-making.summary
Engineering: Casting, machining, forming, welding and 3D printing.

P.title: me-making.q0.q
Engineering: Which process is cheapest per part for very large volumes of plastic parts?

P.title: me-making.q0.x
Engineering: Moulds are costly but each part is cheap.

P.title: me-making.q1.o1
Engineering: Round parts, by spinning the workpiece

P.title: me-making.q1.x
Engineering: The workpiece rotates against the tool.

P.title: me-making.c0.text
Engineering: Most manufacturing either removes material (machining), shapes it (forging, bending, casting), joins it (welding, bolting) or adds it layer by layer (3D printing).

P.title: me-making.c1.text
Engineering: Molten metal is poured into a mould and solidifies in its shape. Engine blocks, pump housings and art bronzes are cast. Die casting forces metal into steel moulds for mass production.

P.title: me-making.c2.text
Engineering: Lathes, mills and drills cut material away to precise shapes. CNC machines follow programmed paths and can hold tolerances of a few hundredths of a millimetre.

P.title: me-making.c3.text
Engineering: Sheet metal is bent, stamped and pressed into shape: car bodies, cans, enclosures. Forging hammers hot metal into shape, giving very strong parts like crankshafts.

P.title: me-making.c4.text
Engineering: Melted plastic is injected into a steel mould and cools in seconds. Moulds are expensive, but each part then costs cents. Most plastic objects around you were made this way.

P.title: me-making.c5.text
Engineering: Welding melts the edges of two metal parts so they fuse. MIG is fast and easy; TIG is precise and clean; stick welding works outdoors. Good welds need clean metal and the right heat.

P.title: me-making.c6.text
Engineering: Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer. FDM printers melt plastic filament; resin printers cure liquid with light; metal printers fuse powder with lasers.

P.title: me-making.c7.text
Engineering: A part that's easy to design can be hard to make. Engineers adapt designs to the process: draft angles for moulding, standard drill sizes, minimum bend radii for sheet metal.

P.title: me-making.c8.text
Engineering: Henry Ford's moving assembly line (1913) cut the time to build a Model T chassis from about 12 hours to about 1.5. Today's factories add robots, sensors and software.

P.title: me-making.c9.text
Engineering: Factories measure parts with gauges, coordinate measuring machines and cameras. Statistical process control spots drift before parts go out of tolerance.

P.title: me-measure.summary
Engineering: Units, precision and making parts fit.

P.title: me-measure.q0.q
Engineering: A tool is consistent but always reads 2 mm too high. It is…

P.title: me-measure.q0.x
Engineering: Consistent but offset from the truth.

P.title: me-measure.q1.o1
Engineering: A part pressed into a slightly smaller hole

P.title: me-measure.q1.x
Engineering: The shaft is slightly larger than the hole.

P.title: me-measure.c0.text
Engineering: Engineering uses SI units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin. Derived units build on them: newton, pascal, joule, watt. Mixing units causes expensive mistakes.

P.title: me-measure.c1.text
Engineering: In 1999 NASA lost a €100-million-plus probe because one team used pound-force seconds and another expected newton-seconds. The spacecraft flew too low into Mars' atmosphere.

P.title: me-measure.c1.viz.items.0.w
Engineering: one team in imperial, one in metric

P.title: me-measure.c2.text
Engineering: Accuracy is how close you are to the true value; precision is how consistent repeated measurements are. A tool can be precise but wrong if it's not calibrated.

P.title: me-measure.c3.text
Engineering: No part is made exactly to size. A tolerance states the acceptable range, such as 20.00 ± 0.05 mm. Tighter tolerances cost more, so use them only where needed.

P.title: me-measure.c4.text
Engineering: Shafts and holes are matched by fit: clearance (slides freely), transition (snug), or interference (pressed in). Standard fit systems like ISO 286 define them, such as H7/g6.

P.title: me-measure.c5.text
Engineering: A tape measures to about a millimetre; calipers to 0.02 mm; micrometers to 0.001 mm. Choose a tool at least ten times finer than the tolerance you're checking.

P.title: me-measure.c6.text
Engineering: 2 m and "2.000 m" mean different precision. Don't report more digits than your measurement supports; a calculator showing 3.14159 doesn't make a rough measurement precise.

P.title: me-measure.c7.text
Engineering: Instruments drift. Calibration compares them against a reference standard and corrects them. Torque wrenches, scales and pressure gauges in industry are calibrated on a schedule.

P.title: me-measure.c8.text
Engineering: When parts stack together, their tolerances add. Ten parts each ±0.1 mm could, in the worst case, be off by ±1 mm together. Statistical tolerancing estimates the realistic spread.

P.title: me-measure.c9.text
Engineering: Pipes, tyres, screens and some bolts still use inches; aviation uses feet and knots. One inch is exactly 25.4 mm.

P.title: me-failure.summary
Engineering: Fatigue, corrosion, creep and famous lessons.

P.title: me-failure.q0.q
Engineering: What causes most mechanical failures in machines and aircraft?

P.title: me-failure.q1.q
Engineering: Why did the Comet airliner crashes lead to rounded windows?

P.title: me-failure.q1.o1
Engineering: Square corners concentrated stress and started fatigue cracks

P.title: me-failure.q2.o1
Engineering: Slow permanent stretching under constant load, especially when hot

P.title: me-failure.c0.text
Engineering: The simplest failure: the load exceeds what the part can carry. Safety factors, good load estimates and checking for misuse prevent most of these.

P.title: me-failure.c1.text
Engineering: Repeated loading, even well below the breaking strength, can grow tiny cracks until a part snaps. Fatigue causes most mechanical failures in machines, aircraft and bridges.

P.title: me-failure.c1.viz.steps.1
Engineering: Tiny crack at a stress point

P.title: me-failure.c2.text
Engineering: Fatigue fractures often show curved "beach marks" on the broken surface, recording how the crack advanced, and a rougher final zone where it finally snapped.

P.title: me-failure.c3.text
Engineering: Corrosion eats away metal, reducing its section and creating stress concentrations. Salt, water and dissimilar metals in contact speed it up.

P.title: me-failure.c4.text
Engineering: Under constant load at high temperature, metals slowly stretch over time. Turbine blades and boiler tubes are designed for creep; even lead pipes and plastic shelves creep at room temperature.

P.title: me-failure.c5.text
Engineering: The de Havilland Comet, the first jet airliner, suffered fatal crashes in 1954 caused by metal fatigue starting at the corners of square openings in its pressurised cabin. Rounded windows became standard.

P.title: me-failure.c6.text
Engineering: In March 2001, a pier of the Hintze Ribeiro bridge over the Douro collapsed, killing 59 people. Years of riverbed erosion, aggravated by sand extraction, had undermined its foundation. Portugal tightened bridge inspections afterwards.

P.title: me-failure.c7.text
Engineering: Many failures come from design errors, poor maintenance, skipped inspections or ignored warnings, not just materials. Good engineering includes checking and learning from near-misses.

P.title: me-failure.c7.viz.items.0
Engineering: Design checks by a second engineer

P.title: me-failure.c8.text
Engineering: Critical systems have backups so one failure doesn't cause disaster: multiple cables on a bridge, two engines on airliners, extra bolts in a joint.

P.title: me-failure.c9.text
Engineering: After a failure, engineers ask "why?" repeatedly to reach the underlying cause, not just the broken part. Fixing only the symptom lets it happen again.

P.title: me-design.q0.q
Engineering: When is fixing a design problem cheapest?

P.title: me-design.q0.x
Engineering: Costs multiply at each later stage.

P.title: me-design.q1.q
Engineering: What is a decision matrix used for?

P.title: me-design.q1.o1
Engineering: Comparing design concepts against weighted criteria

P.title: me-design.q2.o1
Engineering: Conformity with EU safety and other requirements

P.title: me-design.c0.text
Engineering: Good design starts by defining the problem and the requirements clearly: what must it do, under what conditions, at what cost, by when? A great solution to the wrong problem is worthless.

P.title: me-design.c0.viz.items.3
Engineering: Who will use and maintain it?

P.title: me-design.c1.text
Engineering: Design is iterative: define, generate ideas, choose, build a prototype, test, learn, improve. Several loops are normal.

P.title: me-design.c2.text
Engineering: Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves. A clear list helps choose between options and stops scope creep.

P.title: me-design.c3.text
Engineering: Engineers compare options with a decision matrix: score each concept against weighted criteria like cost, weight, reliability and ease of manufacture.

P.title: me-design.c4.text
Engineering: Build quick, cheap prototypes to learn early: cardboard, 3D prints, breadboards. Failing early costs little; failing after production costs a lot.

P.title: me-design.c4.viz.unit
Engineering: relative cost to fix a problem (illustrative)

P.title: me-design.c5.text
Engineering: Tests check the design meets its requirements, including extremes: heat, cold, vibration, water, misuse. Many products are tested to failure to learn their real limits.

P.title: me-design.c6.text
Engineering: Every design balances competing goals: lighter often means more expensive; stronger often means heavier; cheaper may mean shorter life. The engineer's job is the best balance for the purpose.

P.title: me-design.c7.text
Engineering: Standards (EN, ISO, IEC) capture decades of lessons. Following them makes products safer, compatible and legally sellable, like CE marking in Europe.

P.title: me-design.c8.text
Engineering: Drawings, calculations, test reports and decisions must be recorded so others can build, check, maintain and improve the design later.

P.title: me-design.c9.text
Engineering: A product is a system of parts that interact. Changing one part, such as a bigger motor, can affect power supply, heat, weight and cost elsewhere. Systems engineering keeps the whole in view.
